clips.send: A parent sends it to whoever buys Kraft next trip - the shock that it's legally not cheese, and the anger of being tricked.
clips.caption:
Kraft American cheese didn't start as cheese. Back in the 1920s and 30s, a man named Kraft found a way to take ordinary oil, spin it down and break it into tiny molecules until it turned smooth, silky and shelf-stable.

Kevin Trudeau says Kraft had to get permission from Congress just to call the result "cheese" - because by definition, it isn't. It's mostly oil, processed the same way milk is homogenized.

His view: that processed texture you love when it melts is the oil talking, not dairy.

Next time you're in the dairy aisle, what's the first ingredient on the label in your fridge right now?

clips.send: A parent sends it to whoever buys the milk - why store milk lasts three weeks and old-fashioned milk didn't, and the worry underneath it.
clips.caption:
Kevin Trudeau explains why today's milk can sit in a grocery store for three weeks and never go sour, when milk from decades ago spoiled within two or three days and needed a milkman to deliver it fresh.

The process is called homogenization: the fat and milk molecules are broken down and made the same tiny size, so there's nothing left to separate or turn rancid. That's what gives it the longer shelf life.

His view: breaking those molecules down that small isn't the form nature intended you to drink it in - goat, buffalo or cow milk, as it naturally comes.

Next time you're in the dairy aisle, what does "ultra-pasteurized" on the label actually mean?
